blocks.html: Statistics borrows symbols from mathematics and letters from the Greek alphabet. The tables below list the ones used in this book, how to read them aloud, what they mean here, and where they are first explained. You do not need to learn them in advance; come back to this page whenever a symbol stops you.

Symbol Read as Meaning in this book First explained
§ “section” A section of this book: §7.3 is section 7.3 Here
± “plus or minus” A range either side of a value: 11.8 ± 0.6 means 11.2 to 12.4 §3.7
× , · , ÷ “times”, “divided by” Multiplication (× or a raised dot: n·x̄ = n × x̄) and division —
≈ “approximately equal to” The two sides are close but not exactly equal §1.4.4
≠ “not equal to” The two sides differ §3.6.2
< , > “less than”, “greater than” Strict inequalities —
≤ , ≥ “less than or equal to”, “greater than or equal to” Inequalities that include the boundary §1.4.2
√ “square root of” √9 = 3; ∛ is the cube root §2.2.3
x², x³, a^b “x squared”, “x cubed”, “a to the power b” Powers: x² = x × x; a^b is used when the power is long, as in e^(−λ) —
10⁻⁵ “ten to the minus five” 0.00001 (one divided by 10⁵) —
∞ “infinity” Without limit §5.7.2.3
∝ “is proportional to” Changes in fixed ratio with §7.2
→ , ⟹ , ⇒ “gives”, “implies” Leads to, or follows from; in a causal diagram, an arrow (→ or ←) points from cause to effect (§11.6.1); ↔︎ means “corresponds to” §1.1.2
n!, C(n, k) “n factorial”, “n choose k” n × (n − 1) × … × 2 × 1, e.g. 4! = 24; C(n, k) is the number of ways of choosing k items from n §5.7.1.2
Σ “sigma”, “the sum of” Add up everything that follows: Σx = x₁ + x₂ + … + xₙ §2.2.1
Π “pi (capital)”, “the product of” Multiply everything that follows §13.2.3
|x| “absolute value of x” x without its sign: |−3| = 3 §2.3
P(A) “P of A” The probability of event A §5.1
| “given” P(A | B): the probability of A given that B has happened §5.3
~ “is distributed as” X ~ Binomial(n, p): X follows a binomial distribution §5.7.1.2
e, exp “e”, “exponential” The constant 2.718…, the base of natural logarithms; exp(x) = e raised to the power x, which undoes ln §5.7.1.3 (exp: §2.2.3)
ln, log “natural log”, “log” The logarithm to base e (ln), or to base 10 (log₁₀) where stated §2.2.3

Symbol Read as Meaning in this book First explained
x₁, x₂, xᵢ “x one”, “x i” The first, second, i-th value; the small letter below is a label, not a power §2.2.1
x̄, ȳ “x bar”, “y bar” The mean of a sample of x (or y) values §1.3
p̂, ŷ “p hat”, “y hat” An estimate or a predicted value (the “hat” marks something calculated from data) §1.3, §12.2
p “p” A proportion or probability; also the p-value of a test (the context makes clear which) §1.3, §8.5
n, N “n”, “N” The number of observations in a sample (n) or a population (N) §2.2.1
H₀, H₁ “H nought”, “H one” The null and alternative hypotheses §8.2
E(X) “expected value of X” The long-run average of a random quantity §3.6.2, §5.6.1
Var(X), SD, SE “variance”, “standard deviation”, “standard error” Measures of spread of values (SD) and of an estimate (SE) §3.6, §3.7, §6.4
s, s² “s”, “s squared” The standard deviation and variance of a sample §3.6.2, §3.7
df “degrees of freedom” The number of values free to vary once constraints are fixed §3.6.3
z, t, F “z”, “t”, “F” Test statistics and the distributions they follow §5.7.2.2.1, §5.7.2.3, §5.7.2.5
r, R² “r”, “R squared” Pearson’s correlation in a sample; the share of variation a regression explains §11.2, §12.2.5
b₀, b₁ “b nought”, “b one” Intercept and slope of a regression line fitted to a sample §12.2
n′ “n prime” A modified version of a quantity (here, an adjusted number at risk) §14.4

Greek letters usually stand for population values, which are fixed but unknown; Roman letters stand for what you calculate from a sample (recall §1.3). A few letters have more than one use; the text always says which one it means.

Letter Name Meaning in this book First explained
μ mu Population mean §1.3
σ, σ² sigma Population standard deviation and variance §1.3, §3.6.1
α alpha Significance level: the Type I error rate a test accepts (also the negative binomial dispersion, §13.6, and Cronbach’s alpha, §16.3.1.1) §8.3, §8.4
β beta Probability of a Type II error (§8.3); a regression coefficient in the population, as in β₀, β₁ (§12.2.1) §8.3, §12.2.1
χ² chi-squared The chi-square distribution and test statistic §5.7.2.4
ν nu Degrees of freedom of a t or χ² distribution §5.7.2.3
λ lambda Mean number of events in a Poisson distribution (also an eigenvalue in §16.5) §5.7.1.3
ρ rho Population correlation (§11.2); the intraclass correlation in the design effect (§6.2.6); ρₛ is Spearman’s rank correlation (§11.3) §6.2.6, §11.2
τ, τ² tau Kendall’s rank correlation (§11.3); the between-study variance in meta-analysis (§15.7.3) §11.3
κ kappa Cohen’s kappa, agreement beyond chance §16.3.3.1
φ phi The phi coefficient for two binary variables §11.4
Φ phi (capital) The probability that a standard Normal value falls below a given point §8.4
Δ delta (capital) A true difference between groups, used in power and sample size §8.4
δ delta A small step or change §3.5
ε epsilon The error term of a regression model (§12.2.1); a relative margin of error (§7.3) §7.3, §12.2.1
θ theta The dispersion parameter some software reports for a negative binomial model, θ = 1/α (§13.6); the true effect all studies share in a meta-analysis (§15.7.4) §13.6, §15.7.4
π pi The constant 3.14159… (this book writes a population proportion as p, not π) §1.3
ψ psi The baseline odds within a matched set §13.2.9
